extracted.intended_audience: Citizens/voters of New York and the general public debating ratification of the U.S. Constitution
extracted.subtask_description: A series of political-legal arguments (Federalist Papers Nos. 25–29) defending the proposed Constitution's provisions on military power, militia regulation, and restraints on standing armies. The texts assess risks, practicalities, and institutional checks relevant to national defense and internal coercion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Militia insufficient as sole national defense
rubrics_metrics.description: The doctrine that 'the militia of the country is its natural bulwark, and would be at all times equal to the national defense' is unsound.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: War against a regular and disciplined army requires a force of the same kind; militia valor is often notable but cannot alone establish or maintain national liberty. Considerations of economy, stability, and vigor favor a regular force. The recent war (Revolutionary War) demonstrates that reliance solely on militia nearly cost independence and incurred great expense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid impracticable constitutional restrictions
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not fetter government with restrictions that cannot be observed or that run counter to public necessity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provisions impossible to follow in practice (e.g., absolute prohibitions that necessity later overrides) lead to breaches of fundamental laws, impair reverence for the constitution, and set precedents for other breaches. Historical and contemporary examples (Pennsylvania, Massachusetts, the Lacedaemonian subterfuge with Lysander) show nations ignore rules that conflict with pressing needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit military appropriations to two years (biennial funding restraint)
rubrics_metrics.description: Restrain appropriations of money for military purposes to the period of two years rather than attempt total prohibition of standing armies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Biennial appropriations compel the legislature at least every two years to deliberate, publicly vote, and re-examine the necessity of keeping forces. This invites party scrutiny, mobilizes public attention, enables state legislatures to observe and warn, prevents the executive from being vested with permanent military funds, and thus is a practical and salutary check.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cautionary wording is ineffective as a practical prohibition
rubrics_metrics.description: Language saying standing armies 'ought not' be kept up in time of peace is ambiguous and will be treated as admonitory rather than binding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because such phrasing conflicts with possible exigencies, legislatures would likely interpret it as advisory and set it aside when they judged necessity. Hence, vague or moralistic prohibitions produce little real security.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal authority extended to individuals aids enforcement of laws
rubrics_metrics.description: Extending federal authority to individual citizens (rather than only to states collectively) enables the Union to employ ordinary state magistracy in executing federal laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When federal laws apply to individuals, state legislatures, courts, and officers (bound by oath and 'incorporated into the operations of the national government') can be auxiliary to enforcement, reducing reliance on extraordinary coercive measures and making peaceful execution of laws more probable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Familiarity of federal operations reduces need for force
rubrics_metrics.description: The more intermingled and familiar the federal government's operations are in everyday affairs, the more it will gain public respect and attachment, and the less it will need to resort to force.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Government repeatedly present in ordinary life becomes a habitual object of regard; a distant government rarely influences citizens' affections and thus may require coercion. Extending federal agency into internal matters increases legitimacy and voluntary compliance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Biennial elections and public vigilance check long conspiracies
rubrics_metrics.description: Schemes to subvert liberties require time to mature; frequent (biennial) elections and regular turnovers in representative bodies make sustained conspiracies improbable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Progressive augmentations to create a dangerous army would have to be sustained across successive legislatures; biennial elections introduce variations that break continuity, provide opportunities for detection and public warning, and make long conspiracies unlikely. Public discovery would quickly destroy such projects.

rubrics_metrics.name: State legislatures serve as vigilant guardians against federal encroachment
rubrics_metrics.description: State legislatures, being jealous guardians of citizens' rights, will constantly observe national conduct and be ready to alarm the people and act (voice and arm) if the federal government exceeds proper bounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The presence of active state governments gives an institutional check on national overreach. They can detect danger early, combine resources, communicate with other states, and rally the people to resist encroachments, thus reducing the chance of successful federal usurpation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proportionate use of force in emergencies: militia for local, regular forces for large crises
rubrics_metrics.description: In cases of slight local commotions the militia will be adequate; in insurrections pervading a whole State or for interstate operations, a different (more regular) force may be unavoidable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical instances (Massachusetts, Pennsylvania) show states have raised troops in peace to quell disorders. It is unreasonable to expect militia alone to suppress large, organized resistance or to execute extensive operations such as re-establishing jurisdiction over other territories; the means employed must be proportioned to the mischief.

rubrics_metrics.name: National regulation of militia for uniformity with state roles preserved
rubrics_metrics.description: Uniform organization and discipline of the militia are desirable and can only be accomplished by confiding regulation to the national authority, while reserving to the states the appointment of officers and the authority of training according to Congress's discipline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uniformity enables militia called into national service to act with mutual intelligence and concert and to acquire necessary proficiency sooner. The constitutional clause (to organize, arm, and discipline the militia, reserving to the states appointment of officers and training) balances national coordination with state prerogatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Union preferable to loose confederacies for lawful enforcement without force
rubrics_metrics.description: In a mere confederacy laws have no sanction but force and frequent delinquencies by members; a union that acts upon individuals avoids that defect and is less likely to require force for enforcement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Separate confederacies or a disunited state would face the same or worse problems of enforcement, often needing war and violence to redress member delinquencies. A union that reaches individual citizens and uses ordinary magistracy provides more regular and peaceful means of executing laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geographic extent and resources of the Union constrain the danger of federal despotism
rubrics_metrics.description: The great extent of the country and the distribution of resources make it unlikely the federal government could raise and maintain an army capable of subverting liberties across the whole Union.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distance and size make it hard for a federal army to suppress resistance everywhere; reduced resources initially limit army size; as resources (population, wealth) grow, so do the means of resistance by the people and states. Hence the Union's breadth is an additional security against centralized usurpation.
